content:
is this the intended UX? below is my lean proof for the relatively benign statement:

given two pairs of sets A, B, A', B' such that A = A', B = B', A and B disjoint, A' and B' disjoint, there is an isomorphism between their unions

an essentially one line proof in natural language has suddenly turned into 140 lines of lean. if it was ~50-60 lines it would seem acceptable for a computer proof but this just seems incredibly excessive, especially with the amount of splitting that needs to be done for the constructed bijection. if we use by_cases, we can have h : x.val \in a as a hypothesis so surely there should be some way to collapse forwards x down to just the x.val \in a match arm but i was unable to do so. using split inherently feels bad because you need to rename just to get at the hypotheses plus there is a lot of duplicated work here

import Mathlib.Data.Set.Basic
import Mathlib.Logic.Equiv.Defs
import Mathlib.Tactic.ApplyFun
import Mathlib.Tactic.DefEqTransformations

theorem disjoint_unions_iso (α : Type)
    : ∀a b a' b' : Set α
    , ∀_ : a ≃ a', ∀_ : b ≃ b'
    , a ∩ b = ∅ ∧ a' ∩ b' = ∅
    → ∃_ : ↑(a ∪ b) ≃ ↑(a' ∪ b'), True
    := by
  intro a b a' b' f g ⟨h₁, h₂⟩

  -- these will be nice to use inside forwards
  have f_prop : ∀x : ↑a, ↑(f x) ∈ a' ∪ b' := by
    intro
    left
    apply Subtype.coe_prop
  have g_prop : ∀x : ↑b, ↑(g x) ∈ a' ∪ b' := by
    intro
    right
    apply Subtype.coe_prop

  let forwards (x : ↑(a ∪ b)) : ↑(a' ∪ b') :=
    match Classical.dec (x.val ∈ a) with
    | isTrue h => by
      replace x : ↑a := ⟨↑x, h⟩
      exact ⟨↑(f x), f_prop x⟩
    | isFalse h => by
      have x_in_ab := x.prop
      rewrite [Set.mem_union] at x_in_ab
      let x_in_b := x_in_ab.resolve_left h
      replace x : ↑b := ⟨↑x, x_in_b⟩
      exact ⟨↑(g x), g_prop x⟩

  -- construct Equiv via bijection, deferring the proof of bijection
  use Equiv.ofBijective forwards ?_

  -- declare some similar prop lemmas
  replace f_prop : ∀x, (h : x ∈ a) → ↑(f ⟨x, h⟩) ∈ a' := by
    intro _ _
    apply Subtype.coe_prop
  replace g_prop : ∀x, (h : x ∈ b) → ↑(g ⟨x, h⟩) ∈ b' := by
    intro _ _
    apply Subtype.coe_prop

  -- prove the bijection
  unfold forwards
  constructor
  -- prove injectivity
  · intro x y h
    beta_reduce at h
    split at h
    · rename ↑x ∈ a => xa
      split at h
      -- x ∈ a, y ∈ a
      · rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        rewrite [← Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        -- idk how to do this any other way
        replace h := f.injective h
        rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        rewrite [Subtype.coe_inj] at h
        exact h
      -- x ∈ a, y ∈ b
      · exfalso
        rename ¬↑y ∈ a => nya
        have fx_in_a := f_prop ↑x xa
        have gy_in_b := g_prop ↑y (y.prop.resolve_left nya)
        rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        have fx_in_b := gy_in_b
        rewrite [← h] at fx_in_b
        have fx_in_empty := Set.mem_inter fx_in_a fx_in_b
        rewrite [h₂, Set.mem_empty_iff_false] at fx_in_empty
        exact fx_in_empty
    · rename ¬↑x ∈ a => nxa
      split at h
      -- x ∈ b, y ∈ a
      -- once again, this is the exact same proof as before just with some sets
      -- flipped
      · exfalso
        rename ↑y ∈ a => ya
        have gx_in_b := g_prop ↑x (x.prop.resolve_left nxa)
        have fy_in_b := f_prop ↑y ya
        rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        have gx_in_a := fy_in_b
        rewrite [← h] at gx_in_a
        have fx_in_empty := Set.mem_inter gx_in_a gx_in_b
        rewrite [h₂, Set.mem_empty_iff_false] at fx_in_empty
        exact fx_in_empty
      -- this is the exact proof as x ∈ a, y ∈ a but with g.injective instead of
      -- f.injective
      · rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        rewrite [← Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        -- idk how to do this any other way
        replace h := g.injective h
        rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        rewrite [Subtype.coe_inj] at h
        exact h
  -- prove surjectivity
  · intro x

    -- easy lemma, x ∈ a' ∪ b' → x = f a or x = g b
    have h : (∃a : ↑a, (f a).val = x.val) ∨ (∃b : ↑b, (g b).val = x.val) := by
      by_cases xa' : ↑x ∈ a'
      · obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := f.surjective ⟨↑x, xa'⟩
        left
        exists a
        apply_fun (fun x => x.val) at ha
        exact ha
      · have xb' := x.prop.resolve_left xa'
        obtain ⟨b, hb⟩ := g.surjective ⟨↑x, xb'⟩
        right
        exists b
        apply_fun (fun x => x.val) at hb
        exact hb

    -- split the cases of h
    obtain ⟨z, h⟩ | ⟨z, h⟩ := h
    -- x = f z
    · have z_in_union : ↑z ∈ a ∪ b := by
        rewrite [Set.mem_union]
        left
        exact z.prop
      exists ⟨z, z_in_union⟩
      beta_reduce
      split
      -- z ∈ a (forwards)
      · apply_fun Subtype.val using Subtype.val_injective
        exact h
      -- z ∈ b (forwards)
      · rename ¬↑z ∈ a => h'
        exfalso
        have z_in_a := z.mem
        have z_in_b := z_in_union.resolve_left h'
        have z_in_empty := Set.mem_inter z_in_a z_in_b
        rewrite [h₁, Set.mem_empty_iff_false] at z_in_empty
        exact z_in_empty
    -- x = g z
    · have z_in_union : ↑z ∈ a ∪ b := by
        rewrite [Set.mem_union]
        right
        exact z.prop
      exists ⟨z, z_in_union⟩
      beta_reduce
      split
      -- z ∈ a (forwards)
      · rename ↑z ∈ a => h'
        exfalso
        have z_in_a := h'
        have z_in_b := z.mem
        have z_in_empty := Set.mem_inter z_in_a z_in_b
        rewrite [h₁, Set.mem_empty_iff_false] at z_in_empty
        exact z_in_empty
      -- z ∈ b (forwards)
      · apply_fun Subtype.val using Subtype.val_injective
        exact h
Probably you can get there a lot faster with docs#Equiv.Set.union

i think the point of the exercise is mostly to rely on set theory, and not utilize the fancy "disjoint union of types" feature that Lean has, with perhaps representing functions between sets as functions between lean types

pehaps this theorem would be better rephrased using types and equivalences of types, but ideally i would want it to be presentable to someone who doesn't necessaily understand "Two elements of a lattice are disjoint if their inf is the bottom element."
perhaps with these restraints it is just a bit doomed, but i did just read about next, which can clean up the renaming nonsense
Another way to shorten the proof is to directly construct the inverse function too, then you only need to show the two functions compose in both directions to id

Isn't that just the cost of having a robust type-theory based logically restrained formal proof? Every definition (at the sub UI level) costs information and every manipulation costs even more information. I've got the same thing in my project and was also surprised at the lengths of some proofs, even just basic algebra, which can be solved in a line or two on paper. But the paper solution requires a ton of implicit assumptions, which lean not only will not allow, but exposes to you, forcing you to prove them first. So there's the syntax cost of just expressing things completely and soundly, and then there's the proving cost of not allowing assumptions

I've learned a lot in the last few weeks about just how much of my math I was taking for granted that relied on such assumptions, true or not.

Ian Allen said:

Isn't that just the cost of having a robust type-theory based logically restrained formal proof?

No, this is just a consequence of a beginner writing code. Mathlib has many proofs which are far more complex than this and essentially no proofs in mathlib are more than 100 lines long, indeed most are under 10 lines, so this is very strong evidence that you don't need 140 lines to prove the theorem posted by the OP. What's actually happening is that there are tricks which take time to learn. Of course you learn by writing code! And then by other people golfing your code :-)
oh no. thats bad news for my golf course that I am currently building :D

the main issue is probably that i'm trying to prove classical set-theoretic statements while not converting them to lean's type-theoretic interface, so i should probably spend some time studying the specific type theory interfaces

I don't think that's what Kevin means. For example, you have

      -- x ∈ a, y ∈ a
      · rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        rewrite [← Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        -- idk how to do this any other way
        replace h := f.injective h
        rewrite [Subtype.ext_iff] at h
        push_cast at h
        rewrite [Subtype.coe_inj] at h
        exact h

this could instead be

      -- x ∈ a, y ∈ a
      · simpa [SetCoe.ext_iff] using h

if you want the proof to be more explicit and not use simp, it could be

      · replace h := f.injective <| SetCoe.ext <| Subtype.mk.injEq .. ▸ h
        exact SetCoe.ext <| Subtype.mk.injEq .. ▸ h

Long chains of haves that could be inlined and very basic rewrites are a very inefficient way of working--if by efficiency you want fewer lines of code. There are of course other metrics you could judge by.

Ian Allen said:

No, this is just a consequence of a beginner writing code. Mathlib has many proofs which are far more complex than this and essentially no proofs in mathlib are more than 100 lines long, indeed most are under 10 lines, so this is very strong evidence that you don't need 140 lines to prove the theorem posted by the OP. What's actually happening is that there are tricks which take time to learn. Of course you learn by writing code! And then by other people golfing your code :-)

notably, part of that can be attributed to the fact that as you gain experience, you recognise when proofs longer than 10 lines actually are combinations of various sub-10-line lemmas. so it's not necessarily that you find easier formal proofs, it's just that you recognise how to sensibly portion up your proof into contained chunks. the total length of code needn't go down, actually.

Eric Wieser said:

Probably you can get there a lot faster with docs#Equiv.Set.union

Here's that elaborated on, also cleaning up the statement to use docs#Nonempty instead of "exists true"

import Mathlib

theorem disjoint_unions_iso (α : Type) (a b a' b' : Set α)
    (f: a ≃ a') (g : b ≃ b')
    (h : a ∩ b = ∅) (h' : a' ∩ b' = ∅) :
    Nonempty (↑(a ∪ b) ≃ ↑(a' ∪ b')) := by
  classical
  constructor
  exact
    Equiv.Set.union (by simpa [Set.disjoint_iff] using h) |>.trans <|
    f.sumCongr g |>.trans <|
    Equiv.Set.union (by simpa [Set.disjoint_iff] using h') |>.symm

Ok but if you are pulling the lemmas efficiently out of mathlib, instead of inlining the logic directly.. the effective length of your code is still rather long, including all of those mathlib calls, no? You just can't see it outright in your own files. The point I was making was that formal proofs require a lot of steps that are just taken for granted in more basic "napkin" math (my perspective here is as an engineer/physicist who never did formal proofs before). Like I've got a rational function that I transform with some simple algebra, but in lean I have to deal with defining the rational aspect, casting from Q to Z, telling lean my integers are positive, etc, etc.. a lot of this is just implied and naturally understood when you aren't formalizing everything. Even if you are working with more formal sentences, you still might be handwaving through some of the implications, and lean makes you deal with that.

But yeah, I guess once you know how to write formally on paper, soundly, in the first place, and you learn how to call mathlib efficiently, the comparison between the two is going to be much better than what I am currently doing.
